title: AML Agents Briefing — Thursday, 10 September 2026
script:
ALEX: Welcome to AML Agents Briefing. It's Thursday the tenth of September 2026, and this is your audio overview of the most material AML and financial crime developments across Asia-Pacific today. Full detail, the obligation register, and horizon scanning are all at amlagents dot streamlit dot app.

JORDAN: Big day, Alex. We've got Visa making a move into onchain lending, an agentic payment milestone that has real implications for financial crime controls, and two obligations that are due at the end of this month. Let's get into it.

ALEX: Starting with the lead story. Visa has announced it is combining its proprietary settlement data with onchain lending infrastructure. That is not a theoretical experiment. Visa is embedding decentralised credit mechanics directly into a regulated payment network. For compliance teams, the question this raises immediately is how you assess counterparty risk and transaction monitoring when credit origination, settlement, and lending all occur on-chain but are wrapped inside a Visa-branded product.

JORDAN: So Alex, what does that mean in practice for a bank or payment institution that has Visa as a settlement counterpart?

ALEX: It means your existing correspondent or payment counterpart risk framework may not capture the onchain layer at all. Visa's network gives you a familiar regulated shell, but underneath that shell there is now a decentralised credit mechanism. Your transaction monitoring rules were almost certainly calibrated against traditional card flows. They were not built to interrogate onchain lending events that sit upstream of the settlement instruction you actually see.

JORDAN: That is the key point. If you are head of financial crime at a bank that settles Visa transactions, this week you should be pulling your payment-counterpart risk assessment for Visa and checking whether your methodology has a field for decentralised infrastructure risk. If it does not, add it. Raise this with your technology and transaction monitoring teams before your next risk committee meeting, and ask your compliance technology vendor directly whether their monitoring covers onchain credit origination events, not just the card transaction itself.

ALEX: Moving on, the second story also involves Visa. In September 2026, Visa and Revolut completed what they are describing as the first passkey-authenticated agentic card payment in France. An artificial intelligence agent, acting autonomously, initiated and completed a card payment using a passkey for authentication, without a human approving each individual transaction in real time.

JORDAN: And the financial crime read-across here is significant.

ALEX: It is. Authorised push payment fraud controls, and most transaction monitoring logic, assume a human is present at the point of initiation. When an AI agent initiates the payment, the standard behavioural signals you rely on, things like typing speed, device location, and session duration, either disappear or become meaningless. The agent is always fast, always consistent, and always located wherever the server runs.

JORDAN: So for heads of fraud and AML at electronic money institutions and payment service providers, the action this week is straightforward. Map your existing authorised push payment and card fraud controls against an agentic payment scenario. Identify which of your current behavioural signals assume human presence, and flag those as controls that need redesign. This is not a future problem. Visa and Revolut have just demonstrated it works in production.

ALEX: Now for obligations. Two deadlines are bearing down on listeners this month. The first is the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's annual self-assessment return, due the thirtieth of September. This covers the CY 2024 reporting period and must be submitted via the HKMA-prescribed Excel template. Internal Audit must independently validate the submission before it goes in.

JORDAN: If you are the MLRO or head of compliance at an HKMA-regulated institution, you should already have your draft in internal review. If you do not, today is the day to escalate. Internal Audit validation takes time, and the thirtieth is not a soft deadline. Check the HKMA Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Guideline, specifically Section 11, to confirm your self-assessment scope has not missed any updated guidance issued since you last ran this process.

ALEX: And looking further ahead on the horizon scanning, Australian listeners should note that AUSTRAC has levied a civil penalty of forty-seven million Australian dollars against a major registered Digital Currency Exchange for systemic failures in transaction monitoring, mule-account detection, and suspicious matter report timeliness. That enforcement caps a twelve-month investigation.

JORDAN: The lesson for Digital Currency Exchange compliance officers in Australia is direct. AUSTRAC is now demonstrating that it will pursue full civil penalty proceedings for systemic control failures, not just remediation undertakings. If you have open findings from your last AML and CTF programme review, particularly around transaction monitoring calibration or suspicious matter report timeliness, move those to your board's attention now. Do not wait for your next annual review cycle.

ALEX: Before we close, what are the two or three things listeners should focus on this coming week?

JORDAN: Three things. First, if you are at an HKMA-regulated firm, finalise and submit your Section 11 self-assessment return before the thirtieth. Second, whether you are at a bank, payment institution, or digital currency exchange anywhere in the region, map your transaction monitoring and fraud controls against agentic payment scenarios this week and identify which signals assume human presence. And third, for any institution with Visa as a settlement counterpart, update your counterpart risk assessment to include decentralised infrastructure exposure.

ALEX: All the underlying detail, the full obligation register, and the horizon-scanning feed are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app.

JORDAN: That's your briefing for Thursday the tenth of September. We'll be back tomorrow. Stay sharp.
